head.citation-title: Synergistic mechanism of workability, carbonation efficiency, and mechanical performance in bio-carbonated reactive magnesia cement-stabilized flowable soil
head.abstracts: © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.The conflict among strength development, high carbon emissions, and elevated water content in conventional cement-based flowable stabilized soil (FSS) necessitates innovative low-carbon alternatives. This study introduces bio-carbonation reactive magnesia cement (RMC) technology into FSS systems to elucidate the mechanisms governing the interplay among rheological behavior, carbonation progression, and mechanical performance. Through systematic macro- and micro-scale investigations, the effects of RMC content and urea concentration on the physicochemical evolution of fresh pastes and hardened specimens were examined. The incorporation of the bacterial solution inhibited early-stage RMC hydration, delaying the formation of Mg(OH)₂ gel networks and consequently enhancing paste fluidity while reducing yield stress compared to pure water systems. Both yield stress and plastic viscosity exhibited quadratic decay with increasing fluidity. A synergistic optimization mechanism was identified: moderate urea concentrations (2–3 M) achieved a high urea utilization ratio (UUR) while facilitating the sustained progress of RMC hydration and carbonation reactions. This balanced environment promoted homogeneous nucleation and generated dense carbonation products dominated by hydromagnesite. Such microstructural refinement maximized the degree of carbonation (DC) and yielded superior unconfined compressive strength, reaching up to 6.21 MPa at 28 days. Conversely, excessive urea triggered a cascade of detrimental mechanisms: urease activity inhibition, accelerated early carbonation forming surface reaction barriers, crystal coarsening, and extensive micro-/macro-pore formation from entrapped NH₃ gases—collectively disrupting structural continuity and diminishing both carbonation efficiency and strength. Microstructural evidence confirmed that optimal formulations (10%–15% RMC, 2–3 M urea) produced densely interwoven carbonate networks effectively cementing soil particles. This work provides mechanistic insights for designing next-generation high-performance flowable stabilized materials.

coredata.dc:description: The conflict among strength development, high carbon emissions, and elevated water content in conventional cement-based flowable stabilized soil (FSS) necessitates innovative low-carbon alternatives. This study introduces bio-carbonation reactive magnesia cement (RMC) technology into FSS systems to elucidate the mechanisms governing the interplay among rheological behavior, carbonation progression, and mechanical performance. Through systematic macro- and micro-scale investigations, the effects of RMC content and urea concentration on the physicochemical evolution of fresh pastes and hardened specimens were examined. The incorporation of the bacterial solution inhibited early-stage RMC hydration, delaying the formation of Mg(OH)₂ gel networks and consequently enhancing paste fluidity while reducing yield stress compared to pure water systems. Both yield stress and plastic viscosity exhibited quadratic decay with increasing fluidity. A synergistic optimization mechanism was identified: moderate urea concentrations (2–3 M) achieved a high urea utilization ratio (UUR) while facilitating the sustained progress of RMC hydration and carbonation reactions. This balanced environment promoted homogeneous nucleation and generated dense carbonation products dominated by hydromagnesite. Such microstructural refinement maximized the degree of carbonation (DC) and yielded superior unconfined compressive strength, reaching up to 6.21 MPa at 28 days. Conversely, excessive urea triggered a cascade of detrimental mechanisms: urease activity inhibition, accelerated early carbonation forming surface reaction barriers, crystal coarsening, and extensive micro-/macro-pore formation from entrapped NH₃ gases—collectively disrupting structural continuity and diminishing both carbonation efficiency and strength. Microstructural evidence confirmed that optimal formulations (10%–15% RMC, 2–3 M urea) produced densely interwoven carbonate networks effectively cementing soil particles. This work provides mechanistic insights for designing next-generation high-performance flowable stabilized materials.
coredata.dc:title: Synergistic mechanism of workability, carbonation efficiency, and mechanical performance in bio-carbonated reactive magnesia cement-stabilized flowable soil
